title: Rethinking On-Policy Self-Distillation for Thinking Models
claim: Training-time privileged distillation helps under short budgets via compression, but its advantage shrinks or reverses at long budgets as responses shorten.
layout: 2x3 grid of line plots, columns by model, top accuracy, bottom length
description: A 2x3 grid of line charts with a shared legend banner on top. Columns are Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B (Thinking). The top row plots average pass rate (pass@1 solid, pass@16 dashed) against rollout budget from 4k to 38k tokens. The bottom row plots mean (solid) and median (dashed) response length against the same budget. Three colored series appear in every panel: blue is the base thinking model, gray is the base model given a gold demonstration at eval, and orange is OPSD, trained with the gold demonstration but evaluated without it. Orange sits above blue at short budgets, then falls to or below blue at 32k–38k. Orange response lengths plateau well below blue's. Gray stays high on accuracy and very short on length.
caption: For thinking models, OPSD can improve short-budget performance via compression but can hurt long-budget reasoning. We evaluate OpenThoughts-trained Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and OLMo-3-7B thinking models across rollout budgets. Models are trained with a 4,096-token completion cap and evaluated at generation caps from 4,096 to 38,912 tokens. Top row: pass@1 and pass@16, averaged over AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT25. Bottom row: mean and median response length. OPSD with gold demonstrations often helps at 4k–8k tokens, but the advantage shrinks or reverses at 32k–38k tokens, where responses become substantially shorter than the base model.
abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is a promising approach to recursive self-improvement. In this setting, a model acts as its own teacher when augmented with privileged information, such as a solution to a math problem. Thinking models seem especially well positioned to teach themselves this way, since they can deliberate, verify, and self-correct. Surprisingly, we show that OPSD degrades thinking models on long reasoning traces: across five Qwen3 and OLMo thinking models evaluated on AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT25, privileged-context distillation causes a relative drop of up to 17\% in avg@16 accuracy. The degradation scales with the amount of privileged context withheld from the student and is most pronounced at long rollout budgets, where thinking models otherwise obtain their largest gains. This failure mode extends to distillation from a larger, privileged teacher: on-policy distillation (OPD) improves thinking models, but privileged OPD reverses these gains. Our diagnostics suggest that privileged teacher context reshapes learning at high-entropy forking positions, i.e., rollout positions where multiple continuations remain plausible and may lead to different reasoning paths. Privileged context lowers fork rates in thinking-model rollouts but not in instruction-tuned model rollouts, which may explain the observation that OPSD training helps instruct models more reliably than thinking models.At self-correction branches, privileged OPD penalizes sampled reconsideration tokens that vanilla OPD supports. Consistent with this, thinking models trained with a privileged teacher produce fewer verification, backtracking, and hedging markers, even after length normalization. These findings indicate that applying self-distillation methods to strong thinking models requires further consideration of token-level signal---especially around tokens related to correction and crucial reasoning steps.
